note.text:
Air is a mixture of gases: about 78 % nitrogen, 21 % oxygen, almost 1 % argon, and small amounts of carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Gas–gas mixtures can be separated:
• by fractional distillation of liquid air: air is cooled until it becomes liquid, then warmed slowly; each gas boils off at its own boiling point (nitrogen first, then argon, then oxygen). This gives pure oxygen for hospitals and welding, and nitrogen;
• by absorption: the mixture is bubbled through a liquid that dissolves or reacts with only one gas. For example, sodium hydroxide solution absorbs carbon dioxide from air; limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.

worked_example.problem: How can carbon dioxide be removed from a sample of air?
steps: Bubble the air through sodium hydroxide solution.
The sodium hydroxide absorbs the carbon dioxide; the other gases pass through.
worked_example.answer: Absorption: bubble the air through sodium hydroxide solution.

cards.idea: Air is a mixture of gases, mainly nitrogen and oxygen, with a little argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
example: Nitrogen is the gas with the largest share of the air.

cards.idea: Fractional distillation of liquid air: cool air until it is liquid, then each gas boils off at its own temperature.
example: Pure oxygen for hospitals is made this way.

cards.idea: Absorption: bubble the mixture through a liquid that takes in only one gas.
example: Sodium hydroxide solution absorbs carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.explain: Think: is it many gases separated by boiling point, or one gas taken out by a liquid?

questions.prompt: Why does fractional distillation of liquid air work?

right.text: Each gas in the air has a different boiling point.

wrong.text: Each gas has a different colour.
wrong.explain: The gases are colourless; boiling points are used.
That is not how fractional distillation works.
